props.title: Cherry Falls
props.initialSlug: Teen slasher flips script: virgins are the targets

sections.content: **Cherry Falls** (2000) flips classic slasher conventions by targeting virgins instead of sexually active teens, creating a darkly satirical commentary on the genre's traditional morality. Like **Scream** (1996), it's hyper-aware of horror tropes, but pushes further by making abstinence deadly rather than protective. The film joins other millennial meta-horror entries like **Teaching Mrs. Tingle** (1999) and **Urban Legend** (1998) in deconstructing slasher formulas while maintaining genuine tension.

sections.content: Director Geoffrey Wright brings a distinct style that elevates **Cherry Falls** beyond simple parody. The film's commentary on small-town repression and sexual politics feels especially pointed when compared to contemporaries like **I Know What You Did Last Summer** (1997). Brittany Murphy delivers a compelling lead performance that grounds the more outlandish elements, similar to the way Jamie Lee Curtis anchored **Halloween** (1978) with relatable humanity amid supernatural terror.

The film's climactic "virginity party" scene exemplifies its satirical bite, pushing the absurdity of teen slasher conventions to their logical extreme. This approach influenced later genre-bending horror films like **Jennifer's Body** (2009) and **The Cabin in the Woods** (2012), which similarly played with and subverted audience expectations of horror movie "rules." sections.content: **Cherry Falls** arrived at a crucial moment when teen horror was transitioning from the post-**Scream** boom toward more psychological territory. Films like **Final Destination** (2000) and **Ginger Snaps** (2000) were similarly pushing beyond simple stalk-and-slash formulas. The film's willingness to tackle sexuality head-on influenced later teen horror films like **It Follows** (2014), which also uses horror to explore sexual politics and coming-of-age anxieties.
